parts.problem_md:
How is Mayella Ewell important in the novel?

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
| ### Model answer

Mayella Ewell is a central character in To Kill a Mockingbird despite her limited appearance, as her actions catalyse the major conflict in the novel: Tom Robinson’s trial. Through her character, Harper Lee explores themes of prejudice, isolation, class, and injustice.

Mayella is important because she falsely accuses Tom Robinson of raping her, which sets the novel’s main courtroom drama into motion. This accusation drives the tension in the second half of the novel and provides Lee with a powerful lens through which to examine the racism embedded within the legal system and wider society. Without Mayella’s claim, there would be no trial to challenge Atticus Finch’s moral courage or to reveal the extent of Maycomb’s racial prejudices. The trial forces the children, especially Scout and Jem, to confront uncomfortable truths about their community, shifting their understanding of morality and justice.

Lee also uses Mayella to complicate the theme of prejudice by showing that she is not only a perpetrator but also a victim. As the eldest daughter of the violent and abusive Bob Ewell, Mayella is responsible for caring for her many younger siblings after the death of their mother. Her life is defined by poverty, isolation, and fear. Scout, despite her dislike of Mayella, recognises this, saying, “Mayella Ewell must have been the loneliest person in the world.” This insight shows how Lee encourages readers to view Mayella with a degree of sympathy, even though her actions are morally indefensible. She is a young woman trapped by circumstance, gender expectations, and social class, which adds complexity to her character and emphasises how prejudice operates across different levels.

Mayella’s role in the trial highlights the rigid racial and social hierarchies in 1930s Southern America. Although the Ewells are seen as ‘white trash’ and are among the lowest in Maycomb’s social order, Mayella’s whiteness still places her above Tom Robinson, a black man. This power imbalance enables her accusation to be taken seriously despite clear evidence of Tom’s innocence. Lee uses Mayella to show how deeply racial prejudice is embedded in society — so much so that a white girl’s word automatically outweighs the truth told by a black man. Tom’s only ‘crime’ is feeling sorry for Mayella, which the jury sees as a breach of social boundaries: a black man daring to pity a white woman is unacceptable within Maycomb’s racist values.

However, Lee is also careful to suggest that Mayella’s accusation stems from fear and desperation rather than outright cruelty. When Tom testifies that Mayella kissed him and was caught by her father, it becomes clear that her actions are an attempt to cover up her own breach of racial taboos. In the harsh world she lives in, the punishment for a white woman showing affection to a black man would be severe, particularly from her father, who is implied to be abusive. Tom claims Bob Ewell shouted, “you goddamn whore, I’ll kill ya”, which suggests Mayella may have accused Tom to protect herself from violence. This portrayal creates a sense of tragedy: Mayella sacrifices Tom to survive, further underlining how systemic racism and patriarchy trap individuals in cycles of harm.

Lee adds another layer of complexity to Mayella’s character through her love of beauty and order, seen in the red geraniums she grows outside her run-down home. These flowers suggest a desire for something better than her current life allows. They symbolise a longing for dignity and gentleness in a world that offers her neither. This small detail invites readers to consider the contrast between who Mayella is and who she might have been in a different environment, deepening the sense of wasted potential and reinforcing the novel’s wider critique of injustice.

In conclusion, Mayella Ewell is important not only because she triggers the events that shape the narrative, but because she represents the tangled web of prejudice, poverty and patriarchy. Through her, Lee illustrates how individuals can be both victims and perpetrators of injustice, and how systems of inequality produce tragic outcomes. Mayella’s story reminds us that justice is not always blind, and that truth alone is often not enough to overcome the weight of social prejudice. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 40-mark question. parts.problem_md:
Explore the theme of prejudice in To Kill a Mockingbird.

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
| ### Model answer

In To Kill a Mockingbird, Harper Lee explores the theme of prejudice in many forms — racial, social, and gender-based — showing how deeply embedded it is within the community of Maycomb. Through the experiences of Scout, the trial of Tom Robinson, and the treatment of Boo Radley, Lee critiques the injustice and irrationality of prejudice in 1930s America.

The most obvious and devastating form of prejudice in the novel is racial discrimination. Tom Robinson, a black man, is falsely accused of raping Mayella Ewell, a white woman. Although Atticus presents strong evidence that Tom is innocent, the all-white jury convicts him purely because of the colour of his skin. Tom’s only “mistake” is saying that he felt sorry for Mayella, an expression of empathy that Maycomb’s white community views as offensive and presumptuous. This reaction exposes the rigid racial hierarchy of the town in the Jim Crow era, where black people are expected to remain not only separate (due to segregation) but also subservient. As Scout later reflects, “Atticus had used every tool available to free men to save Tom Robinson, but in the secret courts of men’s hearts, Atticus had no case.” Lee’s use of irony here underlines the tragic consequences of racial bias. Lee further explores the consequences of racial prejudice through characters like Dolphus Raymond. He pretends to be an alcoholic to explain his choice to live with a black woman and mixed-race children. In reality, he drinks Coca-Cola from a paper bag and only pretends to be drunk to give people an excuse they can understand. Raymond tells Scout, “they could never, never understand that I live like I do because that’s the way I want to live.” His actions highlight the pressure to conform to societal norms and the lengths people go to in order to protect themselves from judgement.

Social prejudice is also portrayed through the class divisions in Maycomb. Aunt Alexandra is deeply class-conscious and believes that people should only associate with those of the same social standing. She disapproves of Scout’s friendship with Walter Cunningham, declaring he is “not our kind of folks.” Through Aunt Alexandra, Lee criticises the rigid social hierarchy of the Deep South, where even white families are judged by their wealth and family history. Her hypocritical nature is further exposed during her missionary circle meeting. The ladies express sympathy for the Mruna tribe in Africa while simultaneously making derogatory remarks about the black community in their own town. This moment starkly reveals the disconnect between their public charity and private prejudice.

Another victim of prejudice is Boo Radley, who becomes the subject of fear and gossip simply because he lives a reclusive life. Children in the town, including Scout and Jem, initially see Boo as a “malevolent phantom” and he is blamed for any strange event in Maycomb. However, by the end of the novel, Boo is revealed to be gentle and kind, quietly protecting the children by leaving them gifts and eventually saving them from Bob Ewell. Scout’s growing empathy is captured when she finally meets Boo and says that “he was real nice” and Atticus responds, “Most people are, Scout, when you finally see them.” This moment encapsulates Lee’s central message that prejudice often stems from ignorance and fear of the unknown.

Gender prejudice is another key theme, particularly through Scout’s experiences. As a tomboy, she resists traditional expectations of femininity. She is often told to behave more “ladylike”, especially by Aunt Alexandra, and is excluded from playing with Jem and Dill simply for being a girl. Even as a child, Scout recognises the limitations placed on her because of her gender. Lee uses Scout’s narrative voice to expose the absurdity of such social expectations and to suggest that gender roles are another form of harmful prejudice in Maycomb society.

In conclusion, Lee presents prejudice as a destructive and pervasive force within Maycomb. By exploring racial, social, and gender discrimination, she challenges readers to confront their own biases and consider the harm caused by ignorance and injustice. Through the eyes of Scout, the reader learns that prejudice is not only wrong, but deeply ingrained — and that change begins with understanding and empathy. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 40-mark question. This answer would be placed in the top band (Level 5) because it is a well-structured and assured response that shows a critical approach and perceptive understanding of the text. > > **Commentary** > > The candidate explores the theme of prejudice through a wide range of examples — racial injustice, class divisions, gender roles — and offers insightful interpretations of Lee’s characters and methods. There is a consistent focus on the question throughout, with a well-sustained argument that clearly develops across paragraphs. > > Contextual knowledge is embedded seamlessly, supporting points about Maycomb’s social structure, attitudes and the realities of living in the Jim Crow era. Discriminating textual references, both quotations and paraphrases, enhance the clarity and depth of the analysis. The response balances AO1 and AO4 effectively and shows strong engagement with the text’s themes and moral implications. Overall, this is a confident and mature piece of writing that would meet the criteria for full marks. > **[exam-tip]** > - Keep your focus on the **theme of prejudice** in all its forms (racial, class, gender) > - Refer to a **range of characters** to explore the theme deeply (Tom, Boo, Aunt Alexandra, etc.) > - Integrate **historical context** like the Jim Crow laws where relevant > - Use **concise, relevant quotations** to support your interpretations > - Structure your essay around **clear ideas**, not just a list of characters or events

parts.problem_md:
Explore the theme of growing up in To Kill a Mockingbird.

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
| ### Model answer

In To Kill a Mockingbird, Harper Lee explores the theme of growing up through Scout and Jem’s moral and emotional development. The novel, a bildungsroman, traces their journey from innocence to a deeper understanding of their society, its injustices and their place within it. Set in the fictional town of Maycomb during the 1930s, the novel uses events such as the trial of Tom Robinson, interactions with Boo Radley and lessons from Atticus to show how children grow up by facing uncomfortable truths and by learning empathy.

At the beginning of the novel, Scout is presented as an innocent and imaginative child. Her world is filled with childish superstitions and confusion. She believes Boo Radley is a “malevolent phantom” and is terrified of him without ever having seen him. Her misunderstanding of words like “Absolute Morphodite” and her scorn for Miss Caroline’s teaching methods reflect her immaturity and naivety. These moments show how Scout sees the world in simple, black-and-white terms, unaware of the complexity of human behaviour or society’s expectations. Harper Lee uses Scout’s humorous misunderstandings and childlike perspective to highlight how children start life innocently, absorbing the values and prejudices of those around them.

As Scout grows, she begins to confront Maycomb’s flawed social values, especially during Tom Robinson’s trial. The racist treatment of Tom by Mr Gilmer shocks both Dill and Scout. When Dill begins to cry at the injustice, Mr Raymond tells Scout he is still a child — that he will eventually learn not to react and will simply conform to society’s expectations as he grows up. This moment is a turning point in the children’s development as it shows how growing up in Maycomb means being pressured to accept prejudice as normal. However, Scout resists this, and by the end of the novel, she still retains her empathy, showing Lee’s hope for the next generation.

Atticus plays a central role in teaching Scout and Jem how to grow up morally. His advice to “climb into” another man’s “skin and walk around in it” teaches Scout to develop empathy, which signals her growing maturity. This lesson comes full circle when Scout finally meets Boo Radley. Instead of fearing him, she recognises his kindness and protects his identity, standing on the Radley porch and seeing the world from his point of view. This moment symbolises Scout’s emotional growth: she has moved from superstition to understanding, from childish innocence to compassion.

Jem’s growing up is also a key part of the novel. He begins to distance himself from Scout, insisting she act more mature and sometimes criticising her with comments like “you’re gettin’ more like a girl every day!” His annoyance at childish behaviour signals his transition into adolescence. Further, the trial deeply affects him, shattering his belief in the goodness of Maycomb’s people. The Jim Crow laws legalised segregation and events like the Scottsboro trials inspired the trial of Tom Robinson. When the jury finds Tom Robinson guilty, Jem is devastated and begins to understand the depth of injustice in their community. Jem’s new awareness of the world’s unfairness shows his moral growth, but also his loss of innocence. Lee uses their growth to criticise these injustices while offering hope that the next generation might challenge them.

Gender expectations also shape Scout’s development. Aunt Alexandra disapproves of Scout’s tomboy nature and wants her to act like a “lady”. She criticises Scout for wearing dungarees and discourages her from playing with the boys. These pressures reflect the 1930s Southern setting, where strict gender roles defined women’s behaviour. However, Lee presents Scout’s resistance as admirable, suggesting that growing up does not mean conforming to unjust expectations. Scout begins to realise that she can learn from Alexandra while still maintaining her sense of identity, showing a more mature understanding of compromise.

In conclusion, To Kill a Mockingbird explores growing up as a process of gaining moral awareness, developing empathy and questioning societal norms. Through Scout and Jem, Lee shows how children grow not just physically, but emotionally and ethically, especially when faced with the harsh realities of injustice. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 40-mark question. This answer would be placed in the top band (Level 5) because it is a well-structured and assured response that shows a critical approach and perceptive understanding of the text. > > **Commentary** > > This is an insightful and well-structured response that fulfils the criteria for a top-level answer. The candidate explores the theme of growing up with a consistently thoughtful interpretation of the characters’ development. parts.problem_md:
“Put my bag in the front bedroom, Calpurnia,” was the first thing Aunt Alexandra said. “Jean Louise, stop scratching your head,” was the second thing she said.’

Examine the character of Aunt Alexandra in the novel.

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
| ### Model answer

Aunt Alexandra is a complex and important character in To Kill a Mockingbird as she represents the traditional Southern values of class, gender and racial hierarchy. Through her character, Harper Lee explores ideas of family, prejudice and social conformity. Alexandra both challenges and reinforces the values of Maycomb and her evolving relationship with Scout adds depth to the novel’s treatment of gender and moral awareness.

When Aunt Alexandra first arrives in Maycomb, she is immediately portrayed as imposing and controlling. Her first words are commands: “Put my bag in the front bedroom, Calpurnia… Jean Louise, stop scratching your head”. This shows her need for order and her desire to establish authority within the Finch household. Scout feels imprisoned by her aunt’s expectations, describing her arrival as the moment she “felt the starched walls of a pink cotton penitentiary closing in”. The use of prison imagery illustrates Scout’s resistance to Alexandra’s attempts to impose traditional femininity. Lee presents Alexandra as a product of her time: conventional, proper and deeply concerned with reputation.

Aunt Alexandra is obsessed with family heritage and social status. She believes that “fine folks” are those who have lived on the same land for generations, asserting that “the longer a family had been squatting on one patch of land the finer it was”. This narrow view reflects the rigid class system of the 1930s Deep South, where family history determined social worth. Scout observes that her aunt would “point out the shortcomings of other tribal groups to the greater glory of our own”, which highlights Alexandra’s snobbery and blind loyalty to her social circle.

Her views on class and race are also closely linked. When Scout wants to invite Walter Cunningham to their house, Aunt Alexandra is horrified, saying “he — is — trash” and warning that associating with such people will cause Scout and Jem to pick up their “habits”. This moment reveals Alexandra’s class prejudice and her belief that children should be protected from inferior influences. Likewise, she is disturbed by the children’s close relationship with Calpurnia. Alexandra insists that Calpurnia is no longer needed and is shocked to learn the children have attended her church. These attitudes reflect the racial divisions enforced by Jim Crow laws.

Despite her prejudice, Aunt Alexandra is also presented as caring. She eventually allows Calpurnia to serve her missionary guests after recognising her grace and competence. This small concession signals a softening of her rigid views. Additionally, although she initially believes Atticus’ defence of Tom Robinson brings shame to the family, she shows genuine concern when Tom is killed. Her asking Atticus if the town’s criticism upsets him reveals her inner conflict and perhaps guilt. This emotional moment highlights how even those steeped in prejudice can experience doubt and change.

Aunt Alexandra’s character development is especially visible in her relationship with Scout. Initially, she tries to make Scout behave like a “young lady” criticising her dungarees and tomboy habits. She urges Scout to embrace embroidery and activities that will improve her reputation, such as organising missionary teas. However, by the end of the novel, when Scout is attacked by Bob Ewell, Alexandra’s protective side emerges. She calls Scout “darling” and even brings her overalls, showing a rare moment of acceptance and tenderness. This change suggests that Alexandra begins to value Scout’s individuality over outward appearances.

Scout describes her aunt as having “river-boat, boarding-school manners” and being “an incurable gossip”, yet she also acknowledges that Alexandra “let any moral come along and she would uphold it”. Lee uses these observations to present Alexandra as both comic and serious, as she is someone who clings to outdated customs but also possesses strength and care. She is described as the last of her kind, symbolising the dying values of the Old South that the novel critiques.

In conclusion, Aunt Alexandra is a character who represents the Southern Belle ideal, shaped by a culture of class consciousness, gender expectations and racial prejudice. Through her, Lee examines how these values can be both upheld and questioned within a single individual. Alexandra’s development over the course of the novel, from rigid enforcer of tradition to caring family member, shows that even deeply ingrained beliefs can be challenged by empathy and love. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 40-mark question. This answer would be placed in the top band (Level 5) because it is a well-structured and assured response that shows a critical approach and perceptive understanding of the text. > > **Commentary** > > This essay presents a thoughtful and perceptive exploration of Aunt Alexandra’s character, clearly rooted in the text and fully addressing the contextual demands of the question. The response consistently integrates relevant context, especially relating to gender roles, Southern class values and racial prejudice in the 1930s. The analysis of Alexandra’s views on family status, race and femininity is detailed and mature, with strong close reading of moments such as her reaction to Walter Cunningham and her softening at the novel’s end. Quotes are well-selected and interpreted and the argument flows logically across each paragraph. There is also awareness of how Lee’s narrative methods shape the reader’s response to Alexandra, including Scout’s humorous tone. This is a coherent and insightful response. > **[exam-tip]** > - Focus on **what Aunt Alexandra represents** — social class, gender roles, Southern tradition > - Use **Scout’s reactions** to show how Lee encourages readers to question Alexandra’s views > - Track **how her character changes**, especially in her growing care for Scout > - Weave in **historical context** (Jim Crow laws, gender norms, class hierarchy) as you analyse > - Quote or paraphrase **key turning points**, like her views on Calpurnia and the Cunninghams > - Don’t ignore her **more sympathetic moments** — she’s not one-dimensional

parts.problem_md:
Examine the character of Dill Harris in To Kill a Mockingbird.

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
| ### Model answer

Dill Harris is a vital character in To Kill a Mockingbird, acting as both a source of humour and a contrast to Scout and Jem. Harper Lee uses Dill to explore themes of childhood, family, imagination and moral sensitivity. Though a relatively minor character, Dill plays a major role in helping the reader understand both the innocence of childhood and the moral awareness that the trial of Tom Robinson provokes.

When Scout first meets Dill, she describes him as a “curiosity” because of his unusual appearance and style: “He wore blue linen shorts that buttoned to his shirt, his hair was snow white and stuck to his head like duckfluff”. From the start, Dill is different from the children of Maycomb, both in appearance and background. This difference reflects the context of 1930s Southern America, where communities were often closed and suspicious of outsiders. Maycomb is depicted as a microcosm of this world and Dill’s status as an occasional visitor from Meridian sets him apart, though he quickly becomes part of Scout and Jem’s inner circle. Scout says, “summer was Dill”, which captures how essential he becomes to their shared adventures and emotional growth.

Dill fuels the children’s imagination, particularly their fascination with Boo Radley. He invents “eccentric plans, strange longings, and quaint fancies” which Scout lovingly compares to a “pocket Merlin”. His enthusiasm contrasts with Jem’s increasing maturity and Scout’s practical nature. Dill’s love of make-believe and tendency to tell tall tales, like claiming his father is dead, adds humour, but it also suggests a deeper emotional need. His lies about his father’s identity, including once saying “I haven’t got one,” hint at his unstable home life and desire to be accepted and valued.

Dill’s emotional vulnerability becomes more apparent when he runs away from home and hides under Scout’s bed. He tells Scout that his mother and stepfather “do get on a lot better without me, I can’t help them any”. Dill’s confession highlights his loneliness and need for attention. His arrival at the Finch house is welcomed by Atticus, who treats him with kindness and responsibility, which contrasts sharply with the emotional neglect Dill experiences at home. In this way, Lee uses Dill to explore the differences in parenting styles and the importance of moral role models during childhood.

Dill’s most significant moment comes during Tom Robinson’s trial, which marks a shift from playfulness to moral seriousness. When Mr Gilmer cross-examines Tom with cruelty and disrespect, Dill begins to cry. He says, “It was the way he said it made me sick, plain sick”. Dill’s sensitivity highlights the impact of racism on a young, innocent mind. Unlike Scout, who is beginning to understand how Maycomb works, Dill is horrified by the normalisation of racial injustice. This response positions him as a character who still reacts emotionally to cruelty while others have become numb. Dill could also be considered a mockingbird figure because he has an unhappy home life. He loses his childish innocence when he sees the ugliness of adult prejudice.

Raymond Dolphus comforts Dill by suggesting that children “cry about the simple hell people give other people — without even thinking”. This reinforces the idea that Dill, though imaginative and naive, sees the truth more clearly than many adults. It also reflects the context of the Jim Crow South, where institutional racism was so ingrained that its violence often went unquestioned by white society. Dill’s inability to accept this injustice signals both his decency and his loss of childhood innocence.

In his relationship with Scout, Dill also reveals his softer side. He declares that Scout is “the only girl he would ever love” and becomes her “permanent fiancé”. Their innocent affection adds warmth to the novel, but also reflects traditional gender expectations of the time. Dill and Jem sometimes exclude Scout from their adventures, which frustrates her and reminds readers of the gender roles that even young children internalise.

In conclusion, Harper Lee uses Dill Harris to explore the emotional effects of broken families, the transition from innocence to awareness and the moral complexity of childhood in a deeply prejudiced society. Through Dill’s eyes, the reader is reminded that justice and empathy often come more readily from children than adults. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 40-mark question. This answer would be placed in the top band (Level 5) because it is a well-structured and assured response that shows a critical approach and perceptive understanding of the text. > > **Commentary** > > This is a perceptive and detailed response that successfully captures Dill Harris’ character. The candidate demonstrates consistent focus on the question, offering a well-structured and coherent examination of Dill’s emotional vulnerability, imagination and moral development. parts.problem_md:
‘The law is central to this novel.’

How far do you agree with this view?

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
| ### Model answer

The law is central to To Kill a Mockingbird, functioning not only as a plot device but as a lens through which Harper Lee explores justice, morality and social prejudice in 1930s America. However, the novel also suggests that moral justice can exist outside of legal boundaries, showing that while the law is crucial, it is sometimes not always enough.

Atticus Finch, the moral centre of the novel, is a lawyer who believes in justice and equality before the law. He defends Tom Robinson, a black man falsely accused of raping a white woman, Mayella Ewell. Although Atticus does not usually take on criminal cases, he agrees after being asked by Sheriff Heck Tate, knowing that he will lose. This decision reflects his belief in the importance of giving Tom the best possible defence, regardless of race. He tells Scout: “The one thing that doesn’t abide by majority rule is a person’s conscience”. This shows that, for Atticus, the laws of morality must sometimes guide legal duty.

Tom’s trial is the clearest demonstration of the limits of the law in a racially segregated society. Despite clear evidence that Tom could not have committed the crime as his left arm is useless, he is still found guilty. The all-white jury’s decision reflects the deep racial prejudice ingrained in Maycomb and in the legal system of the southern states of America. This echoes the real-life Scottsboro trials, in which nine Black men were wrongly convicted by biased, all-white juries, despite overwhelming evidence of their innocence. Like Tom Robinson, they were failed by a system that should have protected them.

Yet, there are small signs that the law is beginning to change. One juror in Tom’s trial hesitates, which indicates that Atticus’ argument made some impact. Jem, devastated by the outcome, asks, “How could they do it, how could they?” Jem’s emotional response shows a child’s growing understanding of the law and his disappointment in its failure to deliver justice. Harper Lee uses the trial to show how legal institutions can shape young people’s moral education.

Scout also gains awareness of the law throughout the novel. At first, she sees Atticus’ job as just part of normal life, especially when Walter Cunningham pays legal fees with produce rather than money. But by the end of the novel, she has developed a deeper understanding. When Sheriff Tate insists on protecting Boo Radley by claiming that Bob Ewell “fell on his knife”, Scout agrees, saying that exposing Boo would be “like shootin’ a mockingbird”. This moment symbolises Scout’s growth as she recognises that sometimes moral justice must outweigh legal procedure, especially when the law might harm the innocent.

Atticus himself struggles with this dilemma. When he thinks Jem may have killed Bob Ewell, he insists that the law must take its course. However, when it is revealed that Boo Radley saved the children, Atticus accepts Tate’s fabricated account, agreeing that subjecting Boo to the spotlight of the legal system would do more harm than good. This moment reflects a mature understanding that justice is not always best served by strict legal action. As Tate states, “Let the dead bury the dead”, implying that the community’s sense of morality can sometimes override legal truth.

The law is also shown to be intertwined with prejudice and power. The legal system fails Tom Robinson not because of a lack of evidence, but because of his race. Atticus’ defence is logical, ethical and legally sound but it cannot overcome Maycomb’s racist values. This highlights the limits of a law that is meant to be blind but is shaped by social bias. The novel critiques the way legal systems reflect the flaws of the societies they serve.

In conclusion, the law is central to To Kill a Mockingbird, not just in the literal sense of the courtroom scenes, but in how it shapes the characters’ understanding of fairness, truth and justice. However, Lee also shows that legal justice does not always align with moral justice. Through Atticus, Scout and Jem, the novel encourages readers to consider when following the law is right and when it might be more ethical to challenge or interpret it differently. | |---| > **[mark-scheme]** > This is a 40-mark question. This answer would be placed in the top band (Level 5) because it is a well-structured and assured response that shows a critical approach and perceptive understanding of the text. > > **Commentary** > > This is a sophisticated and focused response that fully addresses the question and consistently integrates relevant textual and contextual knowledge. The candidate presents a clear and convincing argument that the law is central to the novel while also recognising its limitations. The analysis explores the character of Atticus as a moral figure within the legal system and effectively discusses the trial of Tom Robinson as a turning point for both Scout and Jem’s development. Contextual links to Jim Crow laws, racial injustice and the Scottsboro trials are woven seamlessly throughout the essay. The contrast between legal justice and moral justice is well developed, particularly in the analysis of Boo Radley’s protection. Textual references are used selectively and precisely. parts.problem_md:
How does Lee present Atticus Finch in To Kill a Mockingbird?

You must consider the context of the novel in your answer.

**[40 marks]**
parts.solution_md:
### Model answer

Harper Lee presents Atticus Finch as the moral centre of To Kill a Mockingbird: a father and lawyer whose empathy, integrity and quiet courage make him the conscience of a prejudiced town.

Lee first presents Atticus as a moral teacher. He tells Scout that you never really understand a person until you “climb into his skin and walk around in it”. The metaphor of climbing into someone’s skin makes empathy sound active and physical, something you choose to do rather than simply feel. Because the novel is narrated by an adult Scout looking back on her childhood, this lesson carries weight: the reader sees that it shapes the woman she grows into. As a single father raising two children in 1930s Maycomb, where strict ideas about discipline and family were the norm, Atticus’s gentle, reasoning approach already marks him out as different from the town around him.

Atticus’s empathy becomes principle when he agrees to defend Tom Robinson, a black man falsely accused of attacking a white woman. He has no illusions about his chances. He tells Scout that in a Southern court, when it is a white man’s word against a black man’s, “the white man always wins”. This is a clear-eyed admission of how the Jim Crow South worked, where segregation and prejudice meant a black defendant could not get a fair trial. In his closing speech he still reminds the jury that a courtroom should be the one place where all men are treated as equals, whatever their colour. Atticus takes the case knowing he will lose, telling his children that “simply because we were licked a hundred years before we started” is no reason not to try. Lee uses the gap between his certainty of defeat and his decision to fight to show that, for Atticus, doing right matters more than winning.

Lee also uses Atticus to redefine courage itself. After Mrs Dubose dies, he explains that real courage is not “a man with a gun in his hand” but knowing “you’re licked before you begin but you begin anyway”. This definition reflects directly on his own role in the trial. Lee reinforces the idea through the mad-dog scene, in which Atticus reluctantly shoots the rabid Tim Johnson with a single shot. The diseased dog works as a symbol of the madness of racism spreading through Maycomb, and Atticus is the one steady enough to face it. Tellingly, he never boasts about his marksmanship; the children have to learn from Miss Maudie that their father was once the best shot in the county. His refusal to show off makes his courage quieter and, Lee suggests, more genuine.

What makes Atticus admirable is that he is the same person everywhere. Miss Maudie tells the children that “Atticus Finch is the same in his house” as he is on the public streets, capturing the idea that his private and public selves never differ. Lee often builds Atticus through the testimony of other characters like this, which makes his goodness feel earned rather than simply announced by the narrator. He hopes to raise Jem and Scout without catching “Maycomb’s usual disease”, his phrase for the casual racism around them. By calling prejudice a disease, Atticus suggests it is something children absorb from a sick society, so that resisting it takes real, deliberate effort from a parent.

Lee does not present Atticus as faultless. His firm belief in the basic goodness of his neighbours is tested when the all-white jury convicts Tom despite the evidence, and some readers feel his calm patience underestimates how dangerous the town’s racism really is. Even so, his restraint is part of who he is: he insists on treating everyone, including the Ewells who later attack his children, with a dignity they never return. Rather than weakening him, his disappointment makes him more human — a good man trying to hold on to hope in an unjust world.

Through Atticus, Lee argues that real integrity means doing what is right whatever the cost. He is presented less as a flawless hero than as a model of conscience: empathetic, principled and quietly brave in a community that rewards none of these things. In a novel set in the racially divided Deep South, he stands as Lee’s example of the person Maycomb could become, if only it had the courage to climb into another’s skin.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> This is a 40-mark question. This answer would be placed in the top band (Level 5) because it is an assured, well-structured response that shows a perceptive understanding of how Lee presents Atticus and integrates context throughout.
> 
> **Commentary**
> 
> The response stays sharply focused on how Lee presents Atticus — moving through his empathy, his principled defence of Tom Robinson, his redefinition of courage and his consistency — rather than narrating the plot. Textual references are short, well chosen and embedded (“climb into his skin”, “the white man always wins”, “Maycomb’s usual disease”), and the analysis of method is developed rather than just spotted: the skin metaphor, the mad dog as a symbol of racism, and Lee’s habit of building Atticus through other characters’ testimony.
> 
> Context (AO3) is woven into the argument rather than bolted on: the Jim Crow South, segregation and 1930s attitudes to family all support points about Atticus instead of sitting in a separate paragraph. The answer also shows discrimination by acknowledging the limits of Atticus’s optimism, which lifts it securely into Level 5. To push further still, a student could analyse Lee’s adult-Scout narrative perspective a little harder.
> 
> **Other arguments you could consider**
> 
> - A response could focus on Atticus as a parent, comparing his honest, reasoning approach with Aunt Alexandra’s concern for family name and appearances.
> - A response could explore the more critical reading of Atticus as an idealised figure whose faith in gradual change does little to challenge Maycomb’s racist systems directly.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Answer “how” Lee presents Atticus — name her methods (metaphor, symbolism, other characters’ viewpoints), don’t just describe what he does.
> - Keep quotations short and embedded; a phrase like “the white man always wins” is worth more than a long copied-out speech.
> - Weave context into your points — link Jim Crow segregation to specific moments like the trial, never as a separate paragraph.
> - Show range: cover Atticus as father, lawyer and neighbour, not only the courtroom.
> - Use the mad-dog scene to show Lee’s symbolism — Atticus facing the rabid dog mirrors him facing the town’s racism.
> - A confident answer notes Atticus’s limits as well as his virtues; examiners reward a balanced, thoughtful view.
> - Plan five or six points before you write so a 40-mark answer stays focused and covers the whole novel.
